title: MCP Trust and Security
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to identify trust boundaries in an MCP workflow and select controls for consent, authorization, credentials, untrusted input, and audit records. After completing it, learners can review an MCP interaction for security risks they may previously have overlooked.
objectives: Map the participants, data, capabilities, and trust boundaries in an MCP workflow.
Distinguish a component's claimed identity or description from authorization to perform an action.
Apply consent, least privilege, credential isolation, input validation, and audit controls to an MCP workflow.
Review a proposed MCP interaction and explain whether it should proceed, require confirmation, or be denied.

sections.title: Source correction
paragraphs: The prior source entry pointed to a local catalogue file, named an unregistered publisher, and had never been verified. This update replaces that entry with the official MCP specification repository and records a verification date and review cadence.
The correction affects source provenance and review metadata. It does not assert a change to the security guidance in the module.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand ordinary client and server roles, credentials, permissions, and the difference between reading data and changing it. It does not assume knowledge of any particular implementation, and no prerequisite module is required.

MCP connects components that can exchange context and request capabilities. A useful security review therefore asks who is communicating, what data crosses each boundary, what action is requested, and which party has authority to approve that action.

sections.title: Map trust boundaries
paragraphs: Begin by inventorying the user, the component coordinating the interaction, each connected server, downstream services, stored data, and available capabilities. For each connection, record what information can cross it and which actions can be requested.

A trust boundary exists wherever data or authority passes between parties with different owners, policies, privileges, or security assumptions. Crossing a boundary should trigger validation and an authorization decision. A successful connection does not by itself make the other party trusted for every purpose.

Descriptions, instructions, resource contents, and action requests received from another component are inputs. They are not proof that an action is safe or authorized. Evaluate them against local policy and the user's granted authority before use.
sections.callout: Connection is not authorization. Identify the specific data and action allowed at each boundary.

sections.title: Consent and authorization
paragraphs: Consent should be meaningful. Before sensitive data is disclosed or a consequential action is performed, the user should be able to understand what will be shared or done, which party will receive the data or action, and why it is needed.

Apply least privilege by granting only the capabilities and data access required for the current task. Keep read authority separate from write or execution authority when their risks differ. Recheck authorization when the recipient, requested capability, data scope, or expected effect changes.

A component's identity answers who it is. Authorization answers what it may do. Keep these decisions separate so that recognition of a component is not mistaken for permission to perform every action it requests.

sections.title: Protect credentials and process untrusted input
paragraphs: Keep credentials scoped to their intended recipient and purpose. Do not relay a credential to another component merely because that component requests it. A security review should verify who will receive each credential, what authority it carries, and how long it remains usable.

Validate data received across a trust boundary before using it in a sensitive operation. Check that the data has the expected type, size, structure, and destination. Treat instructions embedded in retrieved content as untrusted unless a separate policy explicitly authorizes them.
When a requested action exceeds the current grant, stop and obtain a new authorization decision. Do not silently broaden permissions to make a workflow succeed.

sections.title: Review and audit a workflow
paragraphs: Review an MCP workflow in five steps. First, identify the participants, data, credentials, and capabilities. Second, mark every trust boundary. Third, describe the possible harm if data or authority is misused. Fourth, select controls such as validation, least privilege, explicit confirmation, credential isolation, and denial. Fifth, verify the resulting behavior with both permitted and rejected requests.

Record enough information to reconstruct important authorization decisions, including the requesting party, requested capability, decision, and outcome. Avoid placing secrets or unnecessary sensitive content in those records.

A workflow should proceed without additional confirmation only when the requested action stays within an existing, informed authorization and satisfies local policy. It should request confirmation when the recipient, data scope, capability, or expected consequence changes. It should be denied when required authorization is absent or the request violates policy.

questions.prompt: What should happen when data or authority crosses a trust boundary?
choices: The receiving component should accept it because the connection succeeded.
The crossing should trigger validation and an authorization decision.
All available permissions should be granted temporarily.
The interaction should always be denied.
questions.explanation: The module says that crossing a trust boundary should trigger validation and an authorization decision. A connection alone is not authorization.

questions.prompt: A connected component describes a requested action as safe. What is the correct response?
choices: Treat the description as proof of authorization.
Perform the action if the component has connected before.
Evaluate the request against local policy and the user's granted authority.
Grant write authority whenever read authority already exists.
questions.explanation: Descriptions and requests received from another component are inputs, not proof that an action is safe or authorized.

questions.prompt: When should a workflow obtain a new authorization decision?
choices: Whenever the recipient, capability, data scope, or expected effect changes.
Whenever an audit record is created.
Only when a connection is first established.
questions.explanation: The module directs reviewers to recheck authorization when the recipient, requested capability, data scope, or expected effect changes.
